prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of poetry and prose in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into an inward cosmology of rare formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged: Cărtărescu, credited alone. The exchange has not weakened the core of the case, though it has sharpened what the case depends on. On the common criteria, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding and its sequels) and Solenoid, as publicly known, suggest a voice found nowhere else on the shortlist. Memory, the body and dream are built into one large imaginative structure, and the poetry and essays appear to belong to the same project. If that holds, the whole oeuvre is the object of judgment and not one peak, which is what a Nobel citation should rest on. The case rests on form and sustained imaginative depth, not on national representation, political symbolism or fame. I also do not count the 4-2 split among stated first preferences as evidence of merit, and the chair rightly describes it as only a first-round tally. What keeps me on B047 is that its central claim, large-scale architecture and imaginative construction, can be tested through translation more directly than a prosodic innovation can. That is a point about how confident the committee can be, not a claim that one kind of achievement outranks the other.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unverified. The late books are very long and recursive, and I cannot confirm that their scale is earned and not self-repetition. I also cannot judge how much of the Romanian sentence texture survives translation. Coverage of the early poetry and essays in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so a citation naming poetry and prose together leans on the novels. A second reservation has grown from this round: my ranking of Adonis rests on what I can verify, not on a settled judgment of his merit. If the formal claim for Adonis is real and could be confirmed from the Arabic, changing the language of a whole poetic tradition would be an achievement of the first rank. I could be ranking the better-evidenced candidate above the greater one, and I should not hide that.

responses.point: Olsson argues that building a personal cosmos in prose and changing the language of a poetic tradition are different kinds of achievement, and that the first is not obviously the greater. He says the translation caution I apply to Adonis applies at least as strongly to my own claims about Romanian texture, and that the poems should carry the citation, with the essays as supporting evidence.
responses.response: I accept the first two points. I cannot rank the kinds of achievement against each other, and I do not. My placing of Adonis fifth in the opening ranking reflects how much I can confirm, not a verdict that his work is lesser. I also concede that the translation caution applies to Cărtărescu's verbal texture as much as I have applied it to the Arabic. The difference I still see is narrower. The claim for Cărtărescu rests mainly on construction across volumes, which survives imperfect translation better than prosody and diction do. On wording, I agree that the poems must carry any Adonis citation and that the essays serve as evidence of intellectual depth. If original-language readers confirmed the formal claim, the choice would become a close one, and I would then have to weigh whether Cărtărescu's late scale is shown to be earned.

responses.point: Carlberg says she would move Cărtărescu to first if the quality of the long novels is shown to hold across the whole body of work. She also asks that the same standard of verification be applied to both candidates, and argues that Adonis's influence on later Arabic poetry is publicly documented and not only reputation.
responses.response: I agree on the shared standard and propose it explicitly. Both candidates should be tested by readers of the original or by well-regarded translations, and neither should be exempt because the case sounds familiar. I also accept that documented influence is a fact about the poems' effect and not merely fame. My remaining distinction is that influence shows what the poems did to a tradition but does not by itself show their lasting force. That is the question the committee still cannot answer from translation. Her condition mirrors mine. If close readings showed that the late Cărtărescu volumes merely recycle earlier motifs, I would move to Adonis, not stay put because of my opening ranking.

responses.point: Mattson, in her response to my file, says my own caveat about opacity versus depth is the reason she ranks Can Xue sixth, and that the uniformity of method across a very large output raises the question of development. She also agrees the oneiric imagery in Cărtărescu sits within a long-built cosmos.
responses.response: This persuades me to change something modest in my own file. I ranked Can Xue second and named her my first alternative. The uniformity question is the very one I raised about her, and three colleagues who read her sixth press it. I cannot answer it without Chinese, and translated coverage is partial. I therefore reorder my alternatives. Adonis becomes my first alternative, since he is the serious rival and the question is evidentiary, and Can Xue remains my second as the more radically anti-realist option. I still think her method has not hardened into formula, but I hold that as an impression from partial evidence, not something I can demonstrate.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg's citation stresses that the large works remake the novel on a large scale and credits the poetry with giving the sentences their pressure. He also agrees that the late novels extending the project is a provisional view, and says he would look again at Adonis if the late books proved diluted.
responses.response: I share his conditional, and I would answer the chair's question on citation wording by keeping poetry and prose together, since the poetry appears to be part of the project and not a prelude to it. His wording about remaking the novel claims more than I can support from public knowledge. It also narrows a whole-oeuvre citation to the fiction. A common wording would be the one I now give: a body of poetry and prose in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into an inward cosmology of rare formal ambition. That wording makes no claim about the novel as a genre and leaves room for the committee to reduce the poetry's weight if its translated coverage proves too thin to support the claim.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's verbal texture survives translation from Romanian is unverified, and I have not claimed to have read the corpus directly.

Whether the late, very long volumes deepen the project or only extend it is unresolved. Evidence of repetition would be the same motifs and structures recurring without new formal problems being posed; evidence of extension would be a changed relation among the narrative levels or a changed treatment of the central images. I cannot say which holds without close reading.
Coverage of the early poetry and essays in translation is thin, so a citation naming poetry and prose together may lean on the major novels.

The formal claim for Adonis rests on Arabic prosody, diction and allusion, which I can judge only through translation and secondary accounts. My lower ranking of him reflects evidentiary confidence and not an established judgment of merit, and original-language readings could change that.
Whether Can Xue's consistency reflects depth or formula is open, and translated coverage of her very large output is partial.
No independent verification of any source or work is claimed, and all judgments rest on general public knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: it records no personal, institutional or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own fiction (family drama, love and obsession, WWII-era refugee narratives) and my stated aim of reading broadly across the world's literatures are context only and not evidence for or against any candidate. The DN wording on that aim has not been verified in the original.
